### Executive Summary

U.S. manufacturing reshoring and foreign direct investment (FDI) remained remarkably 
resilient in 2025 despite significant policy uncertainty. Companies continued to invest in 
domestic production to reduce risk, strengthen supply chains, and improve long-term 
competitiveness. 
The Reshoring Initiative recorded approximately 247,000 announced reshoring plus FDI 
manufacturing jobs in 2025, essentially matching 2024 and achieving five years of 240,000+ 
jobs/year. Since 2010, more than 2.3 million manufacturing jobs have been announced 
through reshoring and FDI, reflecting a sustained shift toward U.S.-based production. 
Several important trends emerged during the year: 
• Reshoring and FDI remained strong despite uncertainty surrounding tariffs and industrial policy. 
• Transportation Equipment became the leading industry for announced jobs, reflecting a shift from battery production toward complete vehicle FDI, plus drones and ships. 
• Pharmaceutical investment accelerated significantly, exemplifying renewed domestic investment in critical industries. 
• Tariffs became a major factor in reshoring decisions, although companies continued to emphasize long-term supply chain resilience, Skilled Workforce Availability, and Proximity to Customers as their primary motivations. 
• High-Tech products continued to dominate announced investment, helping to overcome our trade deficit in High-Tech goods. 
• Many companies delayed final investment decisions pending greater policy certainty, suggesting additional upside potential as industrial policy stabilizes. The data indicate that reshoring is increasingly driven by long-term business strategy rather than short-term disruptions. Companies are placing greater value on resilient supply chains, domestic manufacturing ecosystems, skilled labor, and reduced geopolitical risk. The findings in this report provide insight into the evolving competitiveness of U.S. manufacturing and offer policymakers, manufacturers, financial analysts, and economic developers a comprehensive view of the factors shaping future domestic investment. 

### Introduction

The Reshoring Initiative's Annual Report provides an assessment of U.S. manufacturing reshoring and FDI—the two primary mechanisms by which production returns to the United States. Together, these activities represent the replacement of imported goods with domestic production, strengthening U.S. manufacturing capacity, employment, and supply chain resilience. Reshoring and FDI are essentially synonyms for reindustrialization. The report is based on the Reshoring Initiative's proprietary database—the nation's most comprehensive, continuously updated collection of reshoring and FDI manufacturing cases. Using this database, the report examines trends in manufacturing job creation, industries, geographic distribution, source countries, and the business factors influencing investment decisions. It also incorporates findings from the 2025 and 2026 National Reshoring Surveys to provide additional insight into how manufacturers evaluate sourcing and investment decisions. Details on data sources, how cases are selected and counted, and the definitions used to classify reshoring and FDI are provided in the Methodology section at the end of this report. Although the policy environment shifted considerably during 2025, companies continued investing in U.S. manufacturing as they balanced cost, resilience, market access, workforce availability, and geopolitical risk. This report analyzes those developments and identifies the trends most likely to shape manufacturing investment in 2026 and beyond. For organizations requiring more detailed analysis, the Reshoring Initiative’s full case-level database is available for purchase. It is widely used by manufacturers, financial institutions, economic developers, policymakers, and academic researchers.

### Chapter 1. Reshoring and FDI Job Trends

Resilient Manufacturing Investment Despite Policy Uncertainty

A total of 247,000 manufacturing jobs were announced through reshoring and FDI in 2025, essentially matching the strong performance of 2024 and extending one of the most significant periods of domestic manufacturing investment since the reversal of the offshoring trend began in 2010. This resilience is particularly noteworthy given the economic and policy uncertainty that characterized much of 2025. Manufacturers faced evolving tariffs, changing industrial

policies, geopolitical tensions, and continued supply chain uncertainty. While some companies postponed irreversible capital commitments pending greater policy clarity, manufacturers overall continued expanding U.S. production as they sought to strengthen supply chains, reduce risk, minimize tariffs, and improve long-term competitiveness. The underlying strength of the U.S. economy enabled many manufacturers to move forward with investment decisions despite an uncertain operating environment. Increasingly, companies view reshoring and FDI not as a short-term response to disruptions such as the pandemic, but as a long-term strategy to improve resilience, reduce geopolitical risk, and position production closer to customers and key markets. Although annual results fluctuate with large project announcements and changing policy conditions, the long-term trajectory remains firmly positive.

Source: RI Master Data through 1H 2026, with 2025 annualized.

Long-Term Momentum Continues

Since 2010, companies have announced more than 2.8 million U.S. reshoring and FDI jobs. An estimated 1.8 million of these jobs have already been filled, while the remainder are expected to come online over the next several years as committed facilities become operational.

Exhibit 1.2 | Cumulative Jobs Announced, Reshoring + FDI, 2010-2026*

Source: RI Master Data through 1H 2026, with 2025 annualized.

The first one million announced jobs required about a decade to achieve, driven largely by growing recognition that the hidden costs and risks of offshoring often outweighed apparent labor-cost advantages. Growth accelerated dramatically over the past five years. More than 1.3 million additional jobs have been announced as companies have increasingly prioritized the benefits of domestic sourcing over labor-cost differences in making investment decisions.

Reshoring Continues to Outpace Foreign Direct Investment

While both reshoring and foreign direct investment remain important contributors to U.S. 
manufacturing growth, reshoring continued to account for the majority of announced jobs 
in 2025. 
Reshoring announcements totaled approximately 153,000 jobs, representing about 62 
percent of all announced reshoring plus FDI manufacturing jobs, while FDI announcements 
totaled approximately 94,000 jobs.

Reshoring and FDI replace imported goods with domestically produced goods, and thus strengthen U.S. manufacturing capacity and expand domestic supply chains. Domestic companies primarily reshore to reduce offshore risk and improve supply chain resilience, while foreign manufacturers increasingly invest in U.S. production to serve the world's largest consumer market while avoiding tariff impacts. Together, they represent complementary pathways toward U.S. reindustrialization.

Conditional Announcements Suggest Additional Upside

Although 2025 investment remained strong, announced job totals likely understate the full 
level of manufacturing interest during the year. Many companies announced plans to 
expand U.S. manufacturing but made final investment decisions conditional on greater 
certainty around tariffs, trade and tax policy, and other elements of the evolving industrial 
policy framework. 
Of the 64 conditional reshoring and FDI announcements identified in 2025, 14 have already 
converted, either fully or partially, into confirmed manufacturing projects. As policy 
direction has become clearer in 2026, the number of new conditional announcements has 
declined substantially, suggesting that manufacturers are becoming more confident in 
making long-term investment commitments. 

This trend suggests that additional conditional projects may move forward and supports expectations for continued manufacturing investment as policy uncertainty declines—or as companies become increasingly comfortable making long-term decisions despite some remaining uncertainty.

##### 2026 Outlook

Based on announcements through the first half of 2026, the Reshoring Initiative projects 
that approximately 309,000 manufacturing jobs (see Exhibit 1.1) will be announced during 
the year, bringing cumulative announced reshoring and FDI employment since 2010 to 
roughly 2.7 million jobs. 
Continued momentum will depend on industrial policy, access to skilled labor, use of Total 
Cost of Ownership (TCO) in sourcing decisions, and ongoing improvements in U.S. 
manufacturing competitiveness. If those conditions continue to improve, the large number 
of conditional projects announced during 2025 may represent the beginning of another 
significant wave of reshoring and foreign direct investment. 

### Chapter 2. Industry and Technology Trends

The Composition of Manufacturing Investment Continues to Evolve

Transportation Equipment became the largest industry for announced jobs in 2025, while pharmaceuticals accelerated, batteries moderated, and chips were stable. Together, these changes indicate that U.S. manufacturing investment is becoming more diversified across strategic industries rather than concentrated in a single sector.
